chapter3.title: Building Block One: The Leader's Seven Essential Behaviors
chapter3.hook: 7 promises looked signed until Ezra asked who would come back with proof.
chapter3.counterintuition: Agreement nods; commitment signs. The surprise is that the seven behaviors are not traits to admire; they make each promise plain enough to inspect.
chapter3.tryThisNow: Circle one live promise and write one number beside it: how many of the seven behaviors can be seen before the return pass?
chapter3.keyTakeaway: Use the seven behaviors as a short inspection list: tie each promise to a person, a visible measure, and a return pass before agreement counts.

breakdown.fastRead:
7 promises can look signed while no one can show who brings back proof. Ezra sees that in a first annual leadership assessment: each line has support, but the return point is blank.

The seven behaviors fix that false calm. Know the business close up. Insist on realism. Set clear priorities. Follow through. Reward doers. Grow people's judgment. Know yourself. Agreement nods; commitment signs. When a promise has a person, a visible measure, and a return pass, intention stops floating.
breakdown.deepRead:
Behavior makes a promise inspectable because it gives the promise a place to stand. A goal can sound clean in the room, yet stay vague unless someone asks who checks, what fact could change the answer, and when the return happens.

Jack Welch led General Electric from 1981 to 2001. The GE lesson here is not that a chief should collect reports from far away. It is that repeated passes made the business close enough for weak assumptions to be challenged before they hardened. Distance flatters. Close contact makes the miss harder to hide.

Ram Charan, a management adviser known for CEO and board counsel, brings the same pressure through questions. In client reviews, practical business talk forces a neat claim to face a person, a fact already in view, and a return point. The answer may feel slower. It is cleaner.

Ezra's first assessment fails because he rates tone instead of return. If he had treated the miss as a message problem, he would have improved the wording and left the same weak promise intact. The price of vague agreement is a second pass through the same fog.

Who checks, and when? That short question ties people, strategy, and operations without turning the job into a speech. A chief who welcomes early bad news can still be demanding. The demand is simply aimed at reality before the cost grows.
breakdown.fullRead:
The hard case is a smooth first assessment. Ezra and Dana can get every senior person to agree, yet still leave with weak work if the standard asks only whether the room felt aligned. That is why the checklist has to stay behavioral, not personal.

Use the Leader's Seven Essential Behaviors as questions, not slogans. Start with knowing the people and the business. Pair that with realism. Cut the goals to clear priorities. Bring promises back. Reward the doer. Grow judgment in others. Know yourself before bias bends the call. The list matters because each item asks for evidence in public view. Who knows the business well enough to challenge the claim? Which assumption is being protected from daylight? Which few goals deserve attention now? Which promise returns, and who is grown enough to judge without waiting for the top chair?

Larry Bossidy's case shows the reward side of the standard. The lesson is narrow and useful: priorities do not teach much until the pass and the reward system point at the same conduct. If the smooth speaker gets status while the doer brings proof alone, the culture has already learned the wrong rule.

This is also where the method costs something. Fewer priorities mean someone loses a favored project. Early bad news means a senior person may have to admit a bad read. Growing people means the top chair cannot stay the only source of judgment. Know yourself means bias is not a private flaw; it distorts staffing and operating calls. A fast close feels efficient. A false close is expensive.

Kendra's first version of the assessment tries to be fair by rating every promise gently. Ezra cuts it back. He asks which named person knows the business, which fact might prove the claim wrong, and which return point will expose a miss. Had they not done that, the broad agreement would have survived and the weak handoff would have moved forward under a clean title.

Do not use the seven behaviors as a way to punish every miss. A partial answer can be honest if it comes back early and names what is still unknown. The method fails when candor is treated as disloyalty, or when the checklist becomes a form that no one has to face again.

Make the promise answer back. That line keeps the work personal without making it a cult of personality. It is not about sounding tougher. It is about making the promise visible enough that the business can correct it while correction is still cheap.

examples.title: Yellow Pad Return

planSpec.audience: manager tempted to lead from summaries
planSpec.stakes: a broad goal can hide weak ownership
planSpec.requiredBeat: Use Jack Welch at General Electric to show repeated review keeping the business close.

examples.scenario: Ezra asks the question a reader would ask after the annual pass is over: why did the promise hold this time? The trace runs back to Jack Welch at General Electric, where repeated reviews kept the business close. Ezra paid the cost in hours, returning to the weak line until a named person and visible fact sat on the yellow pad.
examples.whatToDo: Ezra starts by tracing the win backward. He asks which person knew the business well enough to challenge the promise before it became a safer summary.
examples.whyItMatters: Ezra pays for close knowledge in time. Repeated passes keep a broad goal from hiding behind distance and rank.

examples.title: Outside The Reward Line

planSpec.domain: customer partner reward shift after operating review
planSpec.audience: leader who wants behavior to change
planSpec.stakes: people copy what the system honors
planSpec.requiredBeat: Use Larry Bossidy to tie priorities to reviews and rewards.

examples.scenario: Jenna is not in the operating review when the rule changes. She hears it later from the customer partner: the next reward will follow the person who brings proof back, not the person who gives the cleanest promise. During Larry Bossidy's 1990s chief executive tenure, the pre-Honeywell merger operating improvement depended on reviews and rewards teaching which priorities counted. From outside the room, Jenna can tell whether the review taught the culture a new rule or only produced another speech.
examples.whatToDo: Jenna checks the reward trail after the review. Name the doer, the proof brought back, and the behavior the next team will copy.
examples.whyItMatters: An outside witness shows whether the system changed. If rewards still follow charm or rank, the stated priority has not reached the culture.

examples.title: Unmet Return Point

planSpec.domain: client review with practical business questions
planSpec.audience: leader who gets neat answers too quickly
planSpec.stakes: a hidden assumption grows costly later
planSpec.requiredBeat: Use Ram Charan client reviews to surface reality through practical dialogue.

examples.scenario: Dana notices the early signal before the client names it: one fact will not sit straight. The target has a person, but the resource line does not match the promise. Ram Charan, the management adviser known for CEO and board counsel, would keep the practical question alive. Dana marks the cold coffee ring beside the gap. The return point is set; the answer is not yet met.
examples.whatToDo: Dana gives you the command: name the one fact that does not fit, assign the return point, and refuse to treat a neat answer as done.
examples.whyItMatters: Dana leaves you the warning: early bad news is data, not disloyalty. Use it before the hidden assumption gets costly.

examples.title: Standard Before Close

planSpec.audience: division lead correcting a first attempt
planSpec.requiredBeat: Use the seven behaviors to turn a broad promise into an observable standard.

examples.scenario: Ezra states the demand before the annual leadership assessment can close: no broad promise passes unless the seven behaviors make it observable. Jack Welch at General Electric is the benchmark for staying close, not praising the summary. Had they not done that, the good tone would have hidden weak responsibility. Kendra loses the easy close and has to return with the person, the fact, and the due return. The standard holds, and speed is the price.
examples.whatToDo: Ezra makes the cost visible: skipping this would let a broad promise pass. He slows the close until one person signs for the return.
examples.whyItMatters: Ezra's cost is the price of a real standard: skipping it buys speed while the same weak handoff survives under better wording.

questions.prompt: A clinic director hears clear agreement on a new discharge goal. Several actions could help. Which comes first, and why?
choices: Ask the senior physician to restate the goal for the clinic so staff know the message is official.
Tie the goal to a named person, visible proof, and a return pass so the promise can be corrected.
Freeze each discharge task until the clinic can write a full rule for every handoff and exception.
questions.explanation: The first move makes the promise inspectable. The physician restatement is tempting, but rank only gives the message a stronger source; it does not make the answer return.

questions.prompt: Your volunteer theater has many priorities before opening night. What maps best from the Bossidy lesson?
choices: Keep adding rehearsal goals until the cast sees how ambitious the production can become before opening night.
Link the top priorities to return passes and recognition, so cast members learn which acts carry weight.
Let the board chair choose the priority list, since the title alone will settle the theater's tradeoffs.
questions.explanation: The Bossidy pattern ties priorities to return and rewards. The chair option borrows rank, but it does not teach the cast which behavior earns weight.

questions.prompt: After a software team missed a launch, the director says the goal sounded strong. Which earlier failure best explains the miss?
choices: The director asked the communications group to rewrite the launch goal for the software team.
The director let the most senior architect approve the goal after the launch language felt persuasive.
The director relied on summary reports instead of repeated close passes through the business facts.
questions.explanation: The GE lesson favors direct, repeated contact with the business. Better wording tempts the director, but the miss came from distance, not weak phrasing.

questions.prompt: When a principal sees early bad news as disloyalty, her team stops raising staffing gaps. What is actually wrong?
choices: Her blind spot is bending people and operating calls before the hard signal can be used.
Her team needs a tighter calendar so each staffing gap gets an administrative due line.
Her deputy should filter the signals first, since rank can protect the principal's time.
questions.explanation: Self-knowledge matters because bias distorts people and operating calls. The calendar choice has a real tool, but it aims at timing while the blind spot remains.

questions.prompt: Several product leads leave a quarterly pass with warm agreement and fast growth. Which action belongs before they count it as done?
choices: Ask the growth lead to certify the pass, since scale shows the product group can carry the promise.
Bring each promise back to a stated return, so agreement becomes something the group sees again.
Wait until later results arrive, then decide whether the conversation mattered.
questions.explanation: Follow-through makes talk answer again. Growth can look persuasive, but scale does not prove the promise has a return point or a person who must bring it back.

questions.prompt: A city agency praised teamwork for months, yet employees copied the people who avoided hard delivery. Which earlier choice caused the drift?
choices: Status and resources went to the smooth talkers, so doers learned the agency's true standard.
The agency let a respected deputy explain teamwork, so staff waited for more official language.
The agency measured citizen demand more often, while the reward signal still pointed elsewhere.
questions.explanation: Rewards teach culture by showing which conduct wins status and support. Measuring demand may be useful, but it misses the agency's wrong reward signal.

questions.prompt: During a neighborhood festival, one coordinator answers every hard call and the helpers stay passive. What maps from capability building?
choices: Let helpers make smaller judgment calls with feedback, so the coordinator is no longer the only brain in the system.
Hand every hard call to helpers at once, so the coordinator proves trust and stops being the bottleneck.
Set firmer event deadlines for helpers, since the calendar is the main device for accountability.
questions.explanation: Capability grows when judgment spreads beyond one person. The handoff-everything option over-corrects; it removes the bottleneck by dumping judgment too fast.

questions.prompt: A warehouse supervisor gets neat updates, but the first bad signal arrives late and costs more. What is the deeper fault?
choices: The supervisor let the shift lead rank the updates, trusting role status to sort the real signal.
The supervisor pushed for more confident personalities, hoping stronger voices would make delays visible sooner.
The supervisor made bad signals feel risky, so hidden assumptions stayed hidden until they were expensive.
questions.explanation: Realism asks for bad signals early. The stronger-personality fix is tempting, but it treats candor as style instead of changing what happens to bad news.

questions.prompt: Suppose a grant committee leaves a planning call with many attractive goals. What should come first before anyone accepts the list?
choices: Cut every goal that lacks an immediate funding win, even before the committee sees the tradeoff.
Let the largest donor choose the list, since outside rank will help the committee focus more quickly.
Name the few priorities that deserve attention, so the committee does not spread effort too thin.
questions.explanation: Clear priorities protect attention and responsibility. The donor option borrows authority, but focus has to come from choosing the few goals the group can truly carry.

reviewCards.front: What are the seven behaviors a senior person uses to make a promise inspectable?
reviewCards.back: Start with Know your people and your business. Add Insist on realism and Set clear goals and priorities. Then Follow through, Reward the doers, Expand people's capabilities, and Know yourself.

reviewCards.front: What does Jack Welch at General Electric teach about knowing the business?
reviewCards.back: Under Jack Welch, General Electric made close knowledge a repeated pass through the business, not distant reporting. The senior person stays near enough to challenge weak assumptions.

reviewCards.front: How did the Bossidy case connect priorities with consequences?
reviewCards.back: Larry Bossidy's case ties priorities to operating passes and rewards. People learned the standard from what came back and what earned status.

reviewCards.front: Why should bad news arrive early?
reviewCards.back: Early bad news lets a leader use the signal while correction is still cheaper. Hidden assumptions get expensive when people learn to protect comfort instead of reality.

reviewCards.front: What changes when follow-through is real?
reviewCards.back: A conversation becomes execution only when the promise is checked again. The return point shows whether the named person brought back the fact the group needed.

reviewCards.front: How do self-knowledge and capability building protect judgment?
reviewCards.back: Self-knowledge keeps blind spots from bending people and operating calls. Capability building spreads judgment so the top chair is not the only source of decisions.

implementationPlan.title: Make the Promise Answer Back
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning agreement into something visible. Use Make the Promise Answer Back by naming who signs, what hard fact returns, and which of the seven behaviors is missing. The skill is not a bigger speech; it is a short pass that can catch weak reality early.

ifThenPlans.context: A promise leaves a call with broad agreement.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a promise leaves a call with broad agreement, then run Make the Promise Answer Back: write who signs for it and what fact returns.

ifThenPlans.context: Bad news arrives before the scheduled return.
ifThenPlans.plan: If bad news arrives before the scheduled return, then ask who checks, and when, then move the return closer.

ifThenPlans.context: A person gets praised for smooth talk.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a person gets praised for smooth talk, then run Make the Promise Answer Back by asking what doer earned status and what proof came back.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Replace one status email today with a circled promise: named person, visible fact, and return time. Send that version before the day ends.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Run one Friday pass: choose a live promise, circle the missing behavior, and move one return point closer.

memorableLines.text: The price of vague agreement is a second pass through the same fog.
memorableLines.why: It names the cost of letting assent stand in for proof.
It turns the whole method into a question a reader can reuse.
It is short enough to say before any pass closes.

chapter5.title: Building Block Three: The Job No Leader Should Delegate: Having the Right People in the Right Place
chapter5.hook: Eliana pauses at the last name and asks what this role will demand first.
chapter5.counterintuition: The staffing call is not cleanup after strategy. It is where the strategy first becomes either believable or soft.
chapter5.tryThisNow: When a key role gets a favorite name, read aloud one sentence: this role will strain at __, and we have seen __ handle that strain.
chapter5.keyTakeaway: Do not hand away the people call. Match each hard role to seen behavior and judgment before the goal becomes a promise others have to carry.

breakdown.fastRead:
Eliana pauses at the last name and asks what this role will demand first. A familiar name is on top. She does not ask who is owed a bigger title. She asks who has already shown the judgment the job will need.

GE Session C (General Electric's structured annual talent reviews during Jack Welch's tenure) is the case. It made role fit a repeated senior duty, not a yearly HR file. Role fit means matching the job's demand with behavior a person has already shown.

That is the job a senior person should not hand away. A goal is only as strong as the person placed under it. Talent is behavior against demand, not a grand title.
breakdown.deepRead:
The move works because a named person makes a promise testable. If Eliana writes the service demand beside Yvonne's name, the group can ask what evidence supports it and when the gap will come back. A broad goal cannot answer those questions.

Use the full pass only for senior, costly, or reset-linked choices. For a small and easy-to-reverse assignment, use the light version: say the demand, name the person, and decide what would prove the fit wrong. The full version fails when it becomes a slow court case or a sponsor's way to protect a favorite. Then choose the smaller screen and keep moving.

IBM's 1993 Gerstner transition (IBM naming Lou Gerstner chief executive as the company moved from a hardware-centered identity toward services and integrated solutions) shows the stakes. A reset does not only need new language. It needs people who can lead the new task when old habits pull back.

Who has shown the judgment this new demand will need? That question keeps the title from doing the thinking. Eliana asks it before the name goes final, because resume strength can open the conversation but cannot close it.

Succession belongs here too. A future handoff is not an admin chore. It is a promise made early. The name written now should match behavior already seen, and the follow-up should say what gap must change before the handoff is real.
breakdown.fullRead:
Reagan starts from a different end: an executive choice that already carries a business bet. The Home Depot's 2000 Nardelli appointment (the company hired Robert Nardelli as chief executive after his GE career for a scaling retail challenge) shows that a hire imports assumptions, not just skill.

The lesson is not that outsiders solve scale, or that insiders should be preferred. The lesson is to say what the hire is supposed to prove. A GE career may signal operating discipline; in The Home Depot case, the match still had to be argued against the retail challenge in front of the company.

A weak people call makes a strong strategy pay for the gap. People watch the selection and learn what seems to count. If the imported pattern fits the need, the signal helps. If the pattern is trusted because of rank or brand, the gap moves into daily operations.

GE Session C adds the repeat. Its annual talent reviews mattered when senior people returned to role fit and named performance gaps. Praise that never changes a choice is not candor. It is cover.

Maverick states the standard this way: do not reward language you cannot connect to behavior. If a person is praised as ready but no one can name a judgment already shown, the word is too light. Development or replacement should stay available while the gap can still be faced.

IBM gives the reset version. In 1993, IBM put Lou Gerstner in the top role during a shift beyond its old hardware center into services plus integrated solutions. Had the reset been handed to people matched only to the old identity, the language could have changed faster than the capability underneath it. That is a way to reason about your own case, not a hidden claim about IBM's details.

The light version matters here. Do not run a full talent argument for every short task. When the choice is low risk and easy to undo, write the demand, put a person beside it, and state the sign that would show a mismatch. Use the heavy version when the role is senior, costly, or tied to a reset. A light screen still has teeth if a named person, a seen behavior, and a follow-up point are written where the group will read them. What it drops is ceremony, not judgment.

What does this role assume about the business? Ask that before you ask who has the best record. The resume can start the file. It cannot make the promise true. The senior duty is to keep the role, the seen behavior, and the follow-up point in one line where the group can read it.

examples.title: Session C After Praise

planSpec.audience: a unit president preparing a talent discussion
planSpec.stakes: polite praise hides a role gap
planSpec.requiredBeat: GE Session C turns a vague talent line into a role-fit test

examples.scenario: After GE Session C ends, talent lead Eliana works backward through the weak choice. GE Session C (General Electric's annual talent reviews during Jack Welch's tenure) did not fail because people were quiet; it failed when praise covered a role gap. A blue pencil mark sits under ready. The follow-up point is set, but no one has yet shown the behavior the harder role needs.
examples.whatToDo: Skip this and the praise becomes the proof. Eliana should turn ready into a short claim: what the role demands, what behavior has been seen, and what gap must come back.
examples.whyItMatters: Leave the gap unnamed and development stays vague. The Session C duty works because the same name returns with evidence, not because the file looks neat.

examples.title: Yvonne Feels The Reset

planSpec.audience: a senior team moving intent into assignments
planSpec.stakes: a bold reset has no matched carrier
planSpec.requiredBeat: IBM's 1993 transition links new work to people able to carry it

examples.scenario: What would someone outside the senior circle feel first? Transition lead Yvonne feels it when an IBM assignment shifts from broad reset language to a person with matched judgment. IBM's 1993 Gerstner transition (chief executive change as IBM moved from hardware identity toward services and integrated solutions) made old status less protective, which is why the match had a cost.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the match and staff inherit a slogan. Yvonne should hold the assignment open until the new demand, the person, and observed judgment fit.
examples.whyItMatters: Let rank settle it and the reset gets cheaper at first, then weaker under strain. The cost paid is familiar status losing cover.

examples.title: The Career Signal

planSpec.audience: a board testing an outside hire
planSpec.stakes: a strong resume hides the operating bet
planSpec.requiredBeat: The Home Depot's 2000 Nardelli appointment carries an operating assumption

examples.scenario: Selection lead Reagan catches the early signal late: the GE career is being treated as the answer. The Home Depot's 2000 Nardelli appointment (a chief executive hired after a GE career for a scaling retail challenge) carried an operating assumption. The folder corner is bent. Had that assumption stayed unnamed, a strong resume could have passed for fit until the miss was hard to move.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the assumption and ambition fills the gap. Reagan should name what the hire is supposed to prove before the career record settles the call.
examples.whyItMatters: Borrowed status travels fast. Context decides late, when the selection has already told people which habits seem to count.

examples.title: Maverick Tests The Gap

planSpec.audience: a team deciding whether praise earns another cycle
planSpec.stakes: candor stalls unless it forces a develop-or-replace choice
planSpec.requiredBeat: GE Session C forces a development-or-replacement choice after the gap is named

examples.scenario: Talent lead Maverick hears the GE Session C praise land inside General Electric's annual talent reviews during Jack Welch's tenure. The gap is now named, so the harder choice is exposed: give the candidate a development assignment tied to the missing behavior, or move someone else into the role. If the compliment closes the file, candor has only delayed the same weak fit.
examples.whatToDo: Make the fork explicit. Either assign development against the named behavior and bring it back, or replace for the role demand.
examples.whyItMatters: A people process earns its force at this point. Vague approval blocks both growth and replacement; a named choice turns the gap into execution work.

examples.title: Eliana Audits The Assignment

planSpec.audience: a senior team checking the reset roster
planSpec.stakes: the services shift has names beside work but not proof of fit
planSpec.requiredBeat: IBM's 1993 Gerstner transition tests whether each reset assignment has seen judgment behind it

examples.scenario: Eliana reviews the IBM reset roster after Lou Gerstner's 1993 arrival. The company is moving from a hardware-centered identity toward services and integrated solutions. One assignment has a name beside it, but the margin shows no observed judgment for that new work. The audit changes the question from who agreed with the reset to who has already shown the capability to carry it.
examples.whatToDo: Mark any assignment that lacks seen judgment for the new task. Keep it open until evidence appears, or reassign it to someone whose behavior fits the work.
examples.whyItMatters: Agreement can masquerade as fit when the roster looks complete. The audit protects the reset by making capability visible before the handoff hardens.

questions.prompt: A hospital launches a new access model. The staffing group keeps early complaints out of the operations talk because they sound negative. Which principle does that break?
choices: Staffing signals belong beside the operating choices, since those calls set how much the access model can actually carry.
Staffing can be tuned after launch, since complaints become clearer once the access model meets real volume.
The most senior clinicians should own the access model, since authority keeps early complaints from slowing the change or raising doubts.
questions.explanation: Early complaints are useful evidence about the staffing ceiling. The launch-first choice sounds disciplined, but it waits until the limit has already formed.

questions.prompt: When a theater hires a director from a strong resume but has no evidence under strain, what should be asked first?
choices: Use the resume as a starting proof, then watch the first hard season for signs of judgment before changes are made.
Ask which past choice proves the candidate can use sound judgment when the job's hard part arrives in practice.
Delay the hire until every stakeholder agrees there is no remaining risk in the choice or its timing.
questions.explanation: The right screen looks for behavior and judgment before the choice closes. The delay answer values caution, but it replaces judgment with a search for certainty.

questions.prompt: Before a grant team accepts a bold delivery promise, it asks HR to rank candidates for the hardest post. What comes first?
choices: Let HR rank the candidates first; the project lead can step in later if delivery starts to slip badly.
Pick the person with the best style for the team, then adjust the promise around that person's strengths and history.
Keep the capability call with the promise holder, while HR helps collect evidence for that final decision.
questions.explanation: The person accepting the promise has to keep the capability judgment. The HR-first option gathers help, but gives away the call until slippage appears.

questions.prompt: Your neighborhood co-op needs a future treasurer before the current one leaves. Which choice maps best?
choices: Wait for the vacancy, then choose whoever handles the first urgent finance task with the least friction and fewest questions.
Ask the current treasurer for a trusted helper and use tenure to settle any close choice.
Prepare someone before the handoff, because future promises depend on judgment already seen in the role.
questions.explanation: Succession is part of delivery because later promises need prepared judgment. The tenure answer feels orderly, but it uses closeness instead of proved fit.

questions.prompt: A museum board recruits an operator with a famous career to manage growth. What should it examine before treating the hire as fit?
choices: Ask what operating assumption the hire brings, then compare that assumption with the museum's growth problem.
Use the famous career to get the hire started, then compare assumptions once growth pressure is visible to the staff.
Measure whether internal candidates feel slighted, then treat that reaction as the main fit signal.
questions.explanation: The selection carries a business bet, so the bet has to match the real growth problem. The quick-start answer borrows trust from career strength.

questions.prompt: Even with full enrollment, a training program gives its hardest cohort to someone with weak judgment. Why is growth not enough?
choices: Scale can hide weak fit; the promise stays fragile when the named person cannot carry the hardest demand.
Scale gives the person more chances to learn, so the gap should wait until demand settles.
A wider support circle can absorb the strain, so the assignment can stay unchanged while help increases over time.
questions.explanation: Growth can mask a poor match, but it does not create the capability the hard post needs. The support answer treats help as a substitute for fit.

questions.prompt: During a library talent discussion before branch assignments renew, a struggling candidate gets broad praise but no named gap. Which fix follows?
choices: Keep the praise and wait for patron strain before naming the gap in a later staffing talk with more evidence from patrons.
Name the gap while choices remain open, so development or replacement can still follow before the role hardens.
Separate praise from role decisions, so the candidate hears support before any hard choice is made.
questions.explanation: Candor matters when it lets a development or replacement choice happen. Waiting for patron strain lets praise keep hiding the gap until the role is harder to move.

questions.prompt: After a city agency agrees on a service reset for a public benefits office, staff want broad goals first and people sorted later. Why is that risky?
choices: Let staff translate the reset after support functions understand the new direction and report back with early lessons.
Protect the familiar posts until the reset has proved demand across the agency and the old habits are stable.
Match people to the new demand before the goal is handed down, or the reset can sound clear and stay loose under strain.
questions.explanation: A reset needs people able to lead the new task, not only a shared goal. The staff-translation answer moves the words along while delaying the match.

questions.prompt: Suppose a youth nonprofit copies an annual talent form from a large company before assigning camp directors. What is missing from the copy?
choices: A cleaner yearly cycle, with each role scored once and stored for the staff file before camp starts.
A repeated fit conversation that keeps fresh evidence beside hard roles after the form is filled.
A chief executive instinct call that can override the cycle whenever familiar names feel safer.
questions.explanation: GE Session C teaches recurrence, not storage. The cleaner-cycle answer looks organized, but it turns a senior duty into a file instead of a live fit call.

reviewCards.front: What people call should stay with the senior person?
reviewCards.back: The senior person keeps the link between role demand and capability. Others can collect evidence, but the final judgment cannot be handed off.

reviewCards.front: What does GE Session C add to the lesson?
reviewCards.back: It makes role fit recurring. General Electric's annual talent reviews during Jack Welch's tenure matter here because the duty comes back instead of ending as HR paperwork.

reviewCards.front: Why does the IBM transition belong in a staffing chapter?
reviewCards.back: IBM's 1993 Gerstner transition moved from hardware identity toward services and integrated solutions. The reset needed people able to lead the new task.

reviewCards.front: What question does The Home Depot case raise?
reviewCards.back: Ask what operating assumption comes with the hire. The 2000 Nardelli appointment after a GE career shows that selection carries a business bet.

reviewCards.front: Why can vague praise harm a staffing choice?
reviewCards.back: It hides the gap that should guide development or replacement. Warm language helps only when it does not block the hard choice.

reviewCards.front: Why is succession part of this same duty?
reviewCards.back: Future promises depend on prepared people. A likely handoff should match someone whose judgment has been seen before the role changes hands.

implementationPlan.title: Match Names To Demands
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Pick one hard role. Read aloud the demand, the person, and the behavior already seen under strain. If the sentence cannot name behavior, keep the choice open or use the light version for a small reversible call.

ifThenPlans.context: Say aloud: This role will strain first at __.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the answer is only a resume, then ask for behavior already seen under that strain.

ifThenPlans.context: Say aloud: Praise has not settled the choice.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the gap is unnamed, then name it before deciding on development or replacement.

ifThenPlans.context: Say aloud: This reset still needs a person who can carry it.
ifThenPlans.plan: If no one has shown judgment for the new demand, then keep the assignment open while evidence is gathered.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Spend 20 minutes reading aloud one live role sentence until it names the strain, the person, and the behavior already seen.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, observe one planned handoff; then note the demand, the named person, and one behavior that supports or weakens the match.

memorableLines.text: Talent is behavior against demand, not a grand title.
